title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A modern fighter radar is no longer a rotating dish; it is a phased array of hundreds of tiny gallium nitride transmit-receive modules, each timed to billionths of a second.
epigraph.author: RF & Microwave Systems Engineering Principle

web_blocks.html: Astra Microwave designs, builds, tests, and ships RF, microwave, and millimeter-wave subsystems from 30 MHz to 40 GHz [7, 8]. Every radar, missile seeker, EW jammer, satellite transponder, and weather station needs an RF front-end. That front-end generates, amplifies, filters, phase-shifts, and receives radio signals. Astra does not build the fighter airframe, rocket motor, or satellite bus [12, 17]. Instead, it builds the high-margin electromagnetic 'eyes and ears' inside them [12, 17].

In FY26, Astra posted ₹1,163 Cr in consolidated revenue and a ₹2,141 Cr standalone order book [1, 13]. By September 30, 2026, the backlog surged to ₹3,937 Cr standalone and ₹4,708 Cr consolidated [3]. Revenue spans four end-market verticals plus the 50:50 Astra Rafael Comsys (ARC) joint venture [1, 12, 13]. By contract type in FY26, standalone sales came from serial production (51.0%), development contracts (27.6%), exports (11.9%), and maintenance and services (9.4%) [13].

web_blocks.takeaway: Domestic defence production now dominates Astra's standalone backlog (99.2% as of Q2 FY27), while the Space & Meteorology verticals are being carved out into Astra Space Technologies Ltd [3, 15].

web_blocks.html: 1. Defence (~54%–67% of revenue; 99.2% of Q2 FY27 standalone backlog): Defence is Astra's core growth engine. It covers airborne and ground radars, EW suites, and missile seekers [3, 12]. Concrete Real-World Example: HAL and DRDO's LRDE needed an indigenous AESA fire-control radar—the Uttam AESA Radar—for the Tejas LCA Mk-1A fighter [17]. They also needed a heavier GaN-based derivative—the Virupaksha AESA Radar—for the Indian Air Force's Su-30MKI Super Sukhoi upgrade [17]. A mechanical dish cannot track multiple agile targets at once or resist modern jamming. Astra partnered with LRDE as a Development-cum-Production Partner (DcPP) to build the plank-based Active Antenna Array Unit (AAAU) [17]. Each unit packs hundreds of GaAs/GaN T/R modules, cold plates, and RF manifolds [17]. Teams assemble each unit in Class 10,000 cleanrooms in Hyderabad and stress-test it to military thermal and vibration specs [7, 8]. Astra then calibrates the array inside its 17m x 15m x 11m Near Field Antenna Test Range (NFTR) [7, 8]. Finally, Astra ships units to HAL under multi-year fixed-price contracts, including the Q2 FY27 HAL radar order that lifted quarterly inflows to ₹2,036 Cr [3, 17].

2. Space Electronics (~9%–11% of FY26 revenue; +88% YoY growth): Astra is one of the few private Indian firms qualified by ISRO for space-grade RF hardware [7, 13, 21]. In orbit, radiation hardness, zero-defect solder joints, and extreme thermal swings leave zero room for repair [7, 13, 21]. Concrete Real-World Example: ISRO's Space Applications Centre (SAC) builds earth-observation and defence Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites like the RISAT and EOS series [12, 13, 21]. Those payloads need high-power Solid State Power Amplifiers (SSPAs), frequency synthesizers, and multi-channel radar receivers that survive launch and vacuum [12, 13, 21]. Astra's space unit builds these sealed hybrid modules with automated die-attach, gold wire-bonding, and 3D X-ray checks [7]. Each module passes burn-in testing under strict MIL and ISRO standards [7]. Contracts are milestone-based, low-volume, high-IP awards where qualification barriers block uncertified rivals [12, 13]. To sharpen capital focus, Astra's board approved an in-principle demerger of Space, Meteorology, and Hydrology into Astra Space Technologies Limited under outgoing MD S. Gurunatha Reddy [15].

3. Meteorology & Hydrology (~2%–16% of revenue): This unit applies Astra's radar physics to civilian weather and water tracking [12, 13]. Concrete Real-World Example: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) places S-band and X-band Doppler Weather Radars (DWRs) along India's cyclone coastlines and Himalayan ridges [12, 13]. These radars measure storm wind speeds and rain density in real time [12, 13]. Astra designs the RF subsystem, pedestal control, and signal processor, installs the radome on-site, and runs multi-year Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMCs) [12, 13]. Government weather tenders arrive in lumpy batches, so this unit swings between 2% and 16% of annual sales [12, 13].

4. Exports & Deemed Exports (~11.9% direct FY26 revenue; historically up to 33%): Astra supplies global defence primes like Rafael, Elbit, and Thales as an offset and subsystem partner [12, 13]. Concrete Real-World Example: When a foreign prime wins an international airborne radar or EW deal, it outsources T/R modules or wideband receivers to Astra's Hyderabad lines [12, 13]. These contracts use build-to-print or build-to-spec terms [12, 13]. Export orders bring faster dollar cash than domestic B2G deals. However, they yield only 12%–16% operating margins because the foreign OEM owns the IP and supplies key MMIC kits [12, 13].

5. Astra Rafael Comsys (ARC) 50:50 Joint Venture: ARC is accounted for via the equity method rather than line-by-line revenue consolidation [5, 11, 13]. Its revenue grew from ₹245.2 Cr (₹18.7 Cr PAT) in FY25 to roughly ₹360 Cr in FY26, with a ₹622–636 Cr year-end order book [5, 11, 13]. Concrete Real-World Example: The Indian Air Force needed jam-resistant Software Defined Radios (SDRs) for fighter and transport aircraft to run encrypted voice and data links. ARC licenses Rafael's waveform IP and builds, integrates, and tests the airborne SDRs in Hyderabad [5, 11, 13]. That structure wins 'Buy Indian (IDDM)' slots that neither partner could capture alone [5, 11, 13].

book_paragraphs: If someone asks you what Astra Microwave actually sells, the temptation is to say 'defence electronics.' That is true, but it is far too vague to be useful. What Astra really sells is the ability to tame electromagnetic waves between 30 megahertz and 40 gigahertz inside environments that try to destroy electronics—fighter jet noses pulling nine Gs, missiles accelerating at supersonic speeds, and satellites baking in orbital vacuum.

Let us walk through the four pillars of the business, plus its Israeli joint venture, with concrete examples so you can picture the hardware leaving the factory floor. Start with Defence, which accounts for roughly 54 to 67 percent of revenue and an astonishing 99.2 percent of the standalone order backlog as of September 2026. Consider the Uttam AESA radar for the Tejas Mk-1A fighter and its heavier gallium-nitride cousin, the Virupaksha radar for the Su-30MKI upgrade. A modern fighter cannot rely on a spinning mechanical dish; it needs an Active Electronically Scanned Array—a flat grid of hundreds of miniature transmit-receive modules that steer radar beams electronically in microseconds. Astra builds those plank-based Active Antenna Array Units in Hyderabad cleanrooms, tests them inside its 17-metre shielded anechoic range, and delivers them to HAL under multi-year production contracts. That single capability explains why Q2 FY27 order inflows surged past 2,036 crore rupees.

The second pillar is Space Electronics, roughly 9 to 11 percent of FY26 revenue and growing 88 percent year-on-year. Picture ISRO's Synthetic Aperture Radar satellites imaging the Earth through cloud cover. Inside those satellites sit Astra's hermetically sealed solid-state power amplifiers and radar receivers. There is no technician in low Earth orbit to swap a failed board, so every gold wire-bond and solder joint is inspected under 3D X-ray and thermally cycled before launch. Because this engineering cadence differs from defence serial production, management is now spinning Space, Meteorology, and Hydrology into a separate entity, Astra Space Technologies Limited.

The third pillar is Meteorology and Hydrology, contributing anywhere from 2 to 16 percent of sales depending on tender timing. Here, Astra applies its radar physics to S-band and X-band Doppler Weather Radars for the India Meteorological Department—tracking cyclones off the Bay of Bengal and cloudbursts in the Himalayas—alongside multi-year maintenance contracts.

The fourth pillar is Exports, representing about 11.9 percent of FY26 direct sales, down from nearly a third during the FY20–FY22 lean domestic years. Here, Astra acts as a build-to-print or build-to-spec supplier of T/R modules to global primes like Rafael, Elbit, and Thales. Exports pay faster in dollars, but because the foreign prime owns the intellectual property, margins sit closer to 12 to 16 percent—half of what domestic IP-led production earns.

Finally, sitting alongside the standalone business is Astra Rafael Comsys, the 50:50 joint venture with Israel's Rafael. ARC builds jam-resistant Software Defined Radios for Indian Air Force cockpits and Army tactical networks. It scaled from 245 crore rupees of revenue in FY25 to roughly 360 crore rupees in FY26, carrying over 620 crore rupees in backlog. Notice, however, that ARC is not immune to execution friction: in FY26, a roughly 2 million dollar foreign-exchange provision weighed on JV profitability even as top-line deliveries accelerated. Together, these five engines explain why Astra's revenue mix—not just its revenue total—drives everything on the income statement.

Let us pause and appreciate how these segments reinforce one another inside Astra's engineering ecosystem. The same gallium nitride power-amplifier physics that Astra masters for an ISRO satellite transponder feeds directly into a fighter aircraft's Active Antenna Array Unit. The same pulse-Doppler signal processing built for a coastal weather radar informs ground-based air-defence surveillance. And the 9.4 percent maintenance and spares stream from fielded systems creates a quiet annuity tail that cushions factory overhead when new tender awards slip by a quarter or two.

Yet the inverse is also true: because 99.2 percent of the Q2 FY27 standalone order book sits in domestic defence, Astra's near-term destiny is overwhelmingly tied to Indian Ministry of Defence, HAL, and BEL execution schedules. Exports have shrunk to a minor contributor in the standalone backlog, meaning Astra has traded currency diversification and faster dollar collections for much higher domestic IP margins. Knowing that trade-off upfront prepares us for the working-capital realities waiting in the next chapter.

Let us walk inside the four revenue pillars so you can see what Astra Microwave actually ships out the factory door. In Defence—which anchors roughly 70 to 75 percent of standalone revenue and 99.2 percent of the ₹3,937 crore standalone order book—the flagship product is not a finished fighter jet or missile, but the RF front-end brain inside it. Think of the Uttam and Virupaksha AESA radar programs for HAL's Tejas and Su-30MKI upgrades: Astra Microwave builds plank-based Active Antenna Array Units (AAAUs) and Solid-State Transmit/Receive (T/R) modules that steer radar beams electronically in microseconds without moving parts.

In Space, the company supplies flight-qualified S-band, C-band, and X-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sub-systems and telemetry transponders for ISRO satellites—hardware that must survive launch vibration and radiation for years without repair. In Meteorology, it builds Doppler Weather Radars and Automatic Weather Stations for the India Meteorological Department. And in Exports plus the 50:50 Astra Rafael Comsys (ARC) joint venture, it manufactures tactical Software Defined Radios (SDRs) and EW sub-systems, with ARC scaling to roughly ₹360 crore in revenue and a ₹622–₹636 crore backlog in FY26.

Notice how each of these four segments carries a distinct engineering cadence and customer rhythm. Defence orders require multi-year prototype qualification before batch production; Space payloads demand zero-defect flight hardware with strict radiation-hardening; Meteorology projects involve turnkey Doppler Weather Radar installation and field maintenance across coastal and mountainous terrain; and the Astra Rafael Comsys joint venture bridges Israeli tactical radio IP with Indian offset manufacturing.

When an investor lumps all of Astra Microwave together as a generic 'defense play,' they miss why gross margins and working capital swing so sharply from year to year. When build-to-print export orders dominate, margins compress toward 12 percent. When indigenous radar and EW subsystems dominate—as they do in the current ₹4,708 crore consolidated backlog—operating margins expand toward 29 to 33 percent.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Notice the hidden hierarchy inside Astra's factory: a rupee of revenue from an indigenous Uttam AESA array carries nearly twice the operating margin of a rupee from an export build-to-print kit. When you and I evaluate Astra, the headline order book number matters far less than the mix inside it.
